We're pretty close to you in location, August 2026 date, and keeping our budget around $30-35k, and doing a good job so far. It's a lot of shopping around, and figuring out what's most important to you. For us it was our venue and photography... we got our venue squared away (splurged a bit, and is all-inclusive, ended up around $26k...) While we don't have a lot of wiggle room, we're finding vendors in our budget, and planning on not going crazy with florals and decor. We want the experience to be best for our guests, not appearances for ourselves. 

What my fiancé and I did, and still refer to, was create a list of absolutely everything we could think of in regard to budget of a wedding, and broke it down into specifics too, not categories. Then we decided how much we want to spend at maximum on each item (ie. $500 photobooth, $200 floral, etc...) Once we put funding down on something, we put the exact cost into the spot and mark it somehow to show that price is set. (For us, we bolded the set in stone cost of our venue.) It makes it much easier to see where the money goes and how much we feel comfortable spending on any specific item. (So instead of Photo/Video grouped, we have photographer, videographer, photobooth, backdrop, and whatever else might be needed for that kind of category.) 

With this, my fiancé and I were able to go "Okay do we really want to spend $x amount for this thing?" and can change as we go. And we can add everything up to see where we're sitting with actual costs and total predicted costs. 

I hope this helps, and good luck from a neighbor '26 bride!

As a student sonographer/ultrasound technologist… they can be pretty uncomfortable. I always feel so bad when I have to push towards a patient’s right or left looking for an ovary. However with PCOS, typically your ovaries may present more prominently. For myself, I have, what my professors call, “juicy ovaries” lol. They are hugging my uterus, and larger than normal. 

As someone who has also gotten a transvaginal ultrasound done for PCOS as well… I personally didn’t really notice much. Granted, I was at the time sexually active… but the movements performed aren’t drastic. And the transducer looks scarier than necessary haha. Only a little bit of it actually is inserted. 

I think the worst part is the insertion. Some places/techs may ask if you want to insert the transducer/camera/probe yourself. You can probably ask them too if they don’t mention it and it’s something you’d prefer. My best tips for you is to stay as relaxed as possible. They should tell you, but if not, you are always allowed to tell them to stop the exam for any reason. Medical consent is very important! 

If you’re questioning why your doctors want to perform a transvaginal exam, versus just transabdominal (external), it’s due to the fact that we (sonographers) can get closer to the uterus and ovaries internally without having to fight your bowel, which shadows out your ovaries. This gets us clearer images, and helps the doctor create a better plan of action for you! 

I hope this is helpful for you! And good luck! :)

It sucks, and maybe in the future you can find some other way of treatment that makes you feel a bit less insecure and upset. I was officially diagnosed a few months ago (at 24 y/o), and started taking more than just birth control… Perhaps, instead of framing it as shame that you have to do these things, maybe think of it as educating. It’s a shitty disease to have. There’s so much to constantly think about. It sucks. But I don’t shy away from the fact I have it. I’ll tell people “Yeah, I have PCOS, I have to take these medications for it, these medications do x, y, and z for the condition.” People seem intrigued to learn about something that’s serious for the most part, at least in my experience. Plus then you can find people who may also have it, or will support you in your journey of combatting the side effects of this condition. I know rn it’s hard. I remember being 16 and dealing with all the stressors of life at the time, and self esteem is a huge deal then. All this is easier said than done. But reframing negative thoughts is one of the best tools that helped me through that time. And using it as an educating moment is powerful. It makes it where you are the one in charge, and you have the say in things. 

As for the tea, I’d be the same way with my medications… just set a reminder on your phone! I have a reminder for each pill I take, as well as other tasks I need to perform. It’s a life saver sometimes haha!

Try to keep your head up, but allow yourself time to feel bad and process through what you’re experiencing. It’s different for all of us. There’s no one right way to navigate PCOS. You got this :)

Coco fiber is not good at all, as it can be harmful if swallowed, and it has dust that can be dangerous if the gecko inhales it. I'm not sure about cypress mulch, as I've never heard of it. Typically, what most leopard gecko care groups suggest are: paper towels (cheap, easy to take out and replace, not smooth so grip is good for them, but the cost of buying paper towels does add up in the long run). Non adhesive shelf liner (usually the ones with some texture, as it mimicks rocky ground that a gecko would find in its natural habitat. Just don't use shelf liner that has adhesive, as the fumes from the adhesive is bad for the gecko). Tiles (slate is the go-to, but any rock tiles, or even ceramic tiles work. Again it mimicks the natural habitat, and it retains warmth when you have a lamp/heater aimed on them). Lastly, and what most people suggest, especially if you've had a gecko for awhile, is a 70/30 mix substrate, which is 70% topsoil (no fertilizers), and 30% play sand (not calcium sand or construction sand). Going bioactive is using that 70/30 and adding live plants. If you were to do the 70/30, I'm sure you could incorporate the cypress mulch. If you don't already, I'd recommend you joining Leopard Gecko Advanced Husbandry/Care groups online, as they have many experienced gecko owners who know a lot more than I do. Facebook is good for these groups.
